newsitem.title: FINLAND: UPM sees growth in specialty products.
newsitem.headline: UPM sees growth in specialty products.

text.p: Finnish forest industry group UPM-Kymmene Oy sees growth in speciality papers and converted products, group chief executive Juha Niemela said on Tuesday.

"Growth will certainly be in these areas -- in speciality papers and converted products -- until we see how the supply and demand situation develops in the main, bigger products," Niemela told a news conference in connection with the 1996 results.
UPM reported 1996 profits before extraordinary items down 43 percent to 3.56 billion markka from 6.28 billion in 1995.
Operating profit at UPM's speciality products division was down to 339 million markka in 1996 from 364 million a year ago.
The division's net sales were almost flat at 3.57 billion markka from 3.53 billion markka in 1995.

"The release paper machine (started at Tervasaari, Finland, last summer) creates opportunities for growth both in its product and for growth in Raflatac, which is our production unit in this area," Niemela said.
Raflatac is the leading producer in Europe of self-adhesive labelstock and is aiming for top rank in the world, Niemela said
Another area targeted for investment is air-laid paper, Niemela said, noting that UPM started a machine for this product in Germany last year.
Air-laid paper is used to make table settings and industrial wipes.
"Investments in these kinds of converted products generate -- for instance in net sales -- many times more than paper machine investments," Niemela said.
"Growth in Raflatac's business area has been in two-digit figures in most years, though it had single-digit growth last year," he said.
UPM-Kymmene would also seek to grow geographically, by boosting capacity utilisation and stepping up its marketing efforts.
"We have scope in capacity -- with last year's capacity utilisation rate below 85 percent," Niemela said.
"We can pick up that 15 percent increase without any investment whatsoever."
"Our stepped-up marketing efforts in Asia are one key to this," Niemela said.
